beads.title: Every tnet long flag dies unless it is spelled with two dashes, where Go takes one or two
beads.description: Go's CLI is built on the standard library `flag` package, which does not distinguish `-hostname` from `--hostname`: `flag.Parse` strips one or two leading dashes and looks the rest up in the same table. Upstream states this outright rather than leaving it to the library — `CleanUpArgs` (cmd/tailscale/cli/cli.go) rewrites BOTH spellings of the two legacy flags it fixes up, matching `arg == "--authkey"`, `arg == "-authkey"`, `strings.HasPrefix(arg, "--authkey=")` and `strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-authkey=")`, and the same four shapes for `--posture-checking`. A function that goes out of its way to handle `-authkey` is a function that expects `-authkey` to arrive. `tnet`'s entry point is `Cli::parse()` (src/bin/tnet.rs `main`) with no pre-pass over `std::env::args`, and clap reads a single leading dash as a short-flag cluster, so a single-dash long flag never reaches the flag it names. Against the release binary: `tnet up -authkey=x` and `tnet up -advertise-exit-node` both exit 2 with `error: unexpected argument '-a' found`, and `tnet up -hostname=probe` is worse — clap reads the leading `-h` as its own help flag, so the command prints `up`'s help and exits **0**. A script that runs that line and checks the exit status is told the node came up, and it never did. This is the broadest instance of the failure this fork keeps fixing one flag at a time (`#302`, `#313`, `#344`): a command line copied from Go's documentation that this fork rejects. Decide where the normalisation lands. The faithful shape is a `CleanUpArgs` equivalent that runs before `Cli::parse()` and rewrites a leading `-` to `--` for any argument whose name is not a defined short flag — which also gives the existing `--authkey`/`--posture-checking` rewrites their natural home, since Go does all three in one function. The decision is the boundary: clap has real short flags (`ping -c`, `ip -4`/`-6`/`-1`, `appc-routes -n`) that must keep meaning what they mean, so the rewrite has to consult the parser's own short-flag set rather than transform every `-x` it sees, and a bare `-` and the `--` end-of-flags marker must both pass through untouched. Port the refusal with it: an unknown flag under either spelling must still be refused, not silently dropped.

beads.title: --posture-checking is an unknown argument, not the former spelling of --report-posture
beads.description: `CleanUpArgs` (cmd/tailscale/cli/cli.go) exists to keep two renamed flags working, and only two: `--authkey` becomes `--auth-key`, and `--posture-checking` becomes `--report-posture`. Each is handled in four shapes — the bare flag with one dash and with two, and the `=value` form with one dash and with two — so `tailscale up --posture-checking`, `-posture-checking`, `--posture-checking=false` and `-posture-checking=false` all reach `newUpFlagSet`'s `report-posture` flag. The rename half of that pair is ported here and the other is not: `#313` gave `up` Go's `--auth-key` spelling (and `login` got it in `#397`), and `tnet` registers `--report-posture`/`--no-report-posture` on both `up` and `set` (src/bin/tnet.rs) with no alias at all: against the release binary `tnet up --posture-checking` exits 2 with `error: unexpected argument '--posture-checking' found`. The pref behind it is fully modelled — `Prefs::posture_checking` is honoured into the engine `Config` (src/ipn/config.rs) and `--config`'s `PostureChecking` key maps to it (src/conffile.rs) — so nothing is missing but the name. The cheap fix is a clap `alias` on the existing flag, which is what `up` already does for `--auth-key` and `--login-server`. Two decisions go with it. First, whether the alias is `visible_alias` (it shows in `--help`, as `--auth-key` does) or a hidden `alias`, given that upstream treats the name as deprecated rather than current — it is not registered as a flag at all, only rewritten. Second, whether the `--no-posture-checking` negation this fork would imply exists, since Go has no such flag: Go spells the off case `--posture-checking=false`, which this fork's boolean pair does not accept. That second question is the same one the single-dash gap raises, and both answers get simpler if the rewrite lands as a shared pre-parse pass rather than as per-flag clap attributes.

beads.title: The mac-app-connector risk has no counterpart, so macOS app-connector setup never warns
beads.description: `risks.go` (cmd/tailscale/cli/risks.go) registers exactly three risk names — `lose-ssh`, `mac-app-connector`, and `all`, which accepts any of them — and `--accept-risk` is documented as taking that list. `presentRiskToUser` prints the risk's message, prints `To skip this warning, use --accept-risk=<type>`, and aborts with `aborted, no changes made` unless the operator confirms at a y/N prompt. Both `up` (cmd/tailscale/cli/up.go, `if env.goos == "darwin" && env.upArgs.advertiseConnector`) and `set` (cmd/tailscale/cli/set.go) raise `riskMacAppConnector` before applying prefs, with a specific message: a macOS app connector is not officially supported because of system limitations, may be unreliable, must not be used for anything mission-critical, and Linux is the recommended platform. This fork ports `lose-ssh` and `all` faithfully — `risk_accepted`, `present_risk_to_user` and Go's abort error are all in src/bin/tnet.rs, and `down`'s refusal (`#336`, `#416`) and `up`'s SSH-toggle gate use them — but knows nothing of `mac-app-connector`. It ships `--advertise-connector` on both `up` and `set`, and it builds and runs on macOS, so the single platform Go warns about is the one where the warning is absent: `tnet up --advertise-connector` on a Mac configures the connector with no prompt and no mention of the limitation. The plumbing is already here, so the work is the condition, the message and the two call sites. Decide two things. Go gates on `env.goos`, the CLI's own build target, which for this fork means `cfg!(target_os = "macos")` in `tnet` rather than anything the daemon reports — worth stating explicitly, because a `tnet` on Linux driving a daemon on a Mac would not warn in Go either. And decide whether `--accept-risk`'s help text and any by-name validation grow to list both types the way Go's does, since an operator who reads `--accept-risk=mac-app-connector` in Go's output should not be told here that the value is unknown.

beads.title: --exit-node=auto:any is refused by name where Go keeps re-resolving it to a live suggestion
beads.description: Go models automatic exit-node selection as a pref, not as a one-shot command: `ipn.Prefs.AutoExitNode` is an `ExitNodeExpression` (ipn/prefs.go), `ipn.ParseAutoExitNodeString` strips the `auto:` prefix registered as `AutoExitNodePrefix`, and `AnyExitNode` ("any") is the only expression defined so far. `tailscale up`/`set --exit-node=auto:any` therefore sets `AutoExitNode` rather than `ExitNodeID`, and the daemon resolves it: `resolveAutoExitNodeLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) asks for the current suggestion and writes the result into `ExitNodeID`, re-running whenever the pick could have gone stale — `refreshAutoExitNode` is set when a link-change delta reports `RebindLikelyRequired`, and the resolution also runs as netcheck reports arrive. Setting `ExitNodeIP` explicitly clears `AutoExitNode`, so the two are mutually exclusive. This fork refuses the whole prefix: `validate_exit_node_selector` (src/ipn/mod.rs) rejects any `auto:`-prefixed selector with a "not supported" error, on `up`, on `set`, and in the declarative `--config` loader (src/conffile.rs). That refusal is the honest choice today — a silent fall-through would have matched a peer literally named `auto:any`, i.e. nothing, and broken exit routing with no error — but the primitive it was waiting for has arrived: `exit-node suggest` ships over the engine's `Device::suggest_exit_node()`, which is the same ranked suggestion Go resolves against. So the gap is now daemon-side wiring, not a missing capability. Decide the re-resolution trigger, which is the substance of the feature rather than the parsing. Go re-picks on link change and on each netcheck report; this daemon has a link-change watcher (src/ipn/linkmon.rs) and already rebuilds on it, but the engine surfaces no netcheck-report event, so a faithful port may have to settle for resolve-at-bring-up plus resolve-on-link-change and say so, or file an ask for the report signal. Decide also whether a stored `auto:any` that resolves to nothing leaves the node with no exit node or holds the previous pick, and port the interaction Go states: naming a concrete exit node clears the expression.

beads.title: A --config file does not lock prefs here, and the fork has Go's default for Locked backwards
beads.description: Go's `ipn.ConfigVAlpha.Locked` (ipn/conf.go) is an `opt.Bool` whose declaring comment reads "whether the config is locked from being changed by 'tailscale set'; it defaults to true". `isConfigLocked_Locked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) implements that default as `b.conf != nil && !b.conf.Parsed.Locked.EqualBool(false)` — locked whenever a config file is in use UNLESS the file says `false` explicitly — and `checkPrefsLocked` makes it the first rule it checks, refusing the whole edit with `can't reconfigure tailscaled when using a config file; config file is locked`. The point is that a declaratively configured node cannot drift: the file is the source of truth and out-of-band mutation is refused, not merged. This fork parses the field and enforces nothing. `src/conffile.rs` declares `locked: Option<bool>` and `unmapped_fields` pushes the warning only when `c.locked == Some(true)`, guarded by a comment asserting that "`Locked: false`/absent is the default (no lock)" — which is the opposite of what upstream documents, so the common case (a real Go config that never mentions `Locked`) gets neither the lock nor the warning that says it is missing. Nothing on the `Request::Set` path in src/server.rs consults the config at all. So `tailnetd --config node.json` followed by `tnet set --hostname other` silently rewrites a pref the file owns, and `tnet up` likewise. Two decisions, and they are separable. The first is the default, which is a compatibility break either way: adopting Go's means an existing deployment that relies on `set` working alongside `--config` starts being refused, so it may want a release note rather than a silent flip. The second is the scope of the refusal — Go gates `checkPrefsLocked`, which is every prefs edit including `up`, while this fork's `reload-config` path deliberately re-reads the file and must keep working. Port the message verbatim if the rule is adopted; if it is declined, the fix is still to correct the comment and warn whenever a config is in use, because the current text tells a reader the wrong thing about upstream.

beads.title: set --shields-up is accepted while Funnel is running, where Go refuses the pair
beads.description: `checkFunnelEnabledLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) is four lines and one of the five children of `checkPrefsLocked`: `if p.ShieldsUp && b.serveConfig.IsFunnelOn() { return errors.New("Cannot enable shields-up when Funnel is enabled.") }`. The rule exists because the two prefs cancel each other out in a way that is invisible from either command's output — shields-up blocks incoming connections, and Funnel exists precisely to accept incoming connections from outside the tailnet, so a node with both set advertises a public endpoint that drops every request. Because the check is in the shared chain, Go applies it to `up`, to `set`, and to any LocalAPI `EditPrefs`, and the error is joined with whatever else failed rather than short-circuiting. This fork has both halves of the state and no check between them. `shields_up` is a first-class pref (src/prefs.rs, `SetOptions::shields_up` in src/ipn/mod.rs, taking the rebuild path because the engine's `Config.block_incoming` is immutable), the daemon owns the serve config, and `serve::funnel_ports` (src/ipn/serve.rs) already computes exactly the predicate Go calls `IsFunnelOn` — it returns the set of ports Funnel is armed on, so non-empty is the answer. `Backend::check_prefs` (src/ipn/mod.rs) ports four of Go's rules and its own rustdoc explains the omission as "Go's ... Funnel-shields rules reference prefs this fork does not model", which was true before serve/funnel shipped and is not true now. Decide where it lands, because `check_prefs` is reached three ways: the `check-prefs` LocalAPI verb (a dry run), the `up` path and the `set` path. Go's answer is one function all three share; this fork's `check_prefs` takes the prospective prefs as arguments and does not currently see the serve config, so it needs the funnel state threaded in. Decide also what the check does about a Funnel armed later: Go re-checks nothing, so a node can still reach the bad state by enabling Funnel after shields-up, and matching that is the faithful port even though it is an obvious follow-up question.

beads.title: A --nickname another profile already holds is accepted, so two profiles can share one name
beads.description: `checkProfileNameLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) refuses a profile rename that would collide: an empty name is always allowed (clearing is free), a name that matches no profile is allowed, and a name whose `ProfileIDForName` lookup returns some OTHER profile's id fails with `profile name %q already in use`. Like the Funnel rule it is a child of `checkPrefsLocked`, so it guards `up`, `set` and `EditPrefs` alike. What it buys is that Go's name lookups are unambiguous: `tailscale switch <name>` resolves against `lp.Name`, and because no two profiles can hold the same one, the answer is unique or absent. This fork writes the name unconditionally. `rename_current_profile` (src/ipn/mod.rs) is the local half of `--nickname` — it ports Go's first arm from `setProfilePrefs` faithfully, registers the current profile in `profiles.json` if it is missing, and writes atomically — but it never asks whether another entry already holds the name, and no caller does either. `profile::resolve_target_to_id` (src/ipn/profile.rs) then resolves by id first and by name second, taking the FIRST hit, which `#301` matched to Go deliberately. The two behaviours sit badly together: first-hit matching is Go's tie-break for a state Go makes unreachable, so here it silently picks one of two identically named profiles instead of refusing the rename that created the pair. `tnet set --nickname work` on two profiles is enough to get there, and `tnet switch work` afterwards is a coin flip the operator cannot see. Port the check with Go's message. The decision is which id the comparison uses, because this fork's profile identity is its id rather than a `LoginProfile` value: the rule must compare against the CURRENT profile's id so that renaming a profile to the name it already has stays legal, which is exactly Go's `id != b.pm.CurrentProfile().ID()`. Decide too whether the check runs on the daemon side, where the profile map lives and where Go puts it, or in `tnet` — the daemon is the faithful answer, since `up` and a future LocalAPI edit must be guarded too, not just the `set` command line.
